title: The major questions doctrine
summary: The major questions doctrine requires clear congressional authorization when an agency claims certain extraordinary powers of substantial economic and political consequence.
notes:
West Virginia describes a contextual trigger involving the history and breadth of the claimed authority and its economic and political significance. Novel assertions under long-existing or ancillary provisions, transformative regulatory consequences, and a poor fit with the agency’s customary responsibilities can prompt the inquiry. The majority required more than a plausible textual basis for EPA’s generation-shifting program and found the necessary clear authorization absent. These are contextual considerations rather than a numerical threshold for how much money, novelty, or controversy makes a question major. (Printed 972–975.)

The assigned materials trace two different uses. King v. Burwell withheld Chevron deference but independently upheld the challenged interpretation. West Virginia applied a narrowing construction and rejected the agency’s program. The casebook then compares student debt relief, OSHA’s broad workplace vaccination-or-testing standard, healthcare-facility vaccination, and the CDC eviction moratorium. The healthcare case illustrates that a consequential action can receive different treatment depending on its statutory and institutional setting. (Printed 937–938, 966, 980–982.)

A separate entry explains the competing justifications. Roberts refers to both separation of powers and likely congressional intent; Gorsuch links the requirement to nondelegation; Barrett understands it as ordinary contextual inference; Kagan challenges a special clear-statement requirement that narrows Congress’s broad language. Those positions should remain attributed. The readings do not supply one uncontested explanation of the doctrine’s legitimacy or exact boundaries. (Printed 977–983.)
